fleet_size_for_rate.note: Wikipedia: ~75 kits sold, 20 completed (initially), 31 Berkuts registered across all variants. FAA registry download 2026-10-24: 26 current US registrations with 'Berkut' in make/model, 2 of them Mobius UAV derivatives -> 24 Berkut airframes. Crude record: 9 NTSB events on ~31 airframes (~30% of fleet).

safety.pattern: RECORD: 9 NTSB events on a ~31-aircraft fleet. Causes: accelerated stall in an airshow max-g turn (prototype, fatal); canard attach bolts left out by builder -> in-flight canard separation (fatal); main-gear failures (N538AJ: hydraulic pump failure and over-centre downlock springs never installed by previous builder; same aircraft had later gear accidents per Wikipedia); engine power loss on approach (N260DG, undetermined per NTSB; Wikipedia says mis-rebuilt fuel pump); dust devil on final flipped aircraft (N600SE); undetermined flight-control malfunction on final (N5439N); turbine fuel controller failure (jet conversion); ignition anomalies on test flight (N567JS); canopy not latched, departed in flight (N976DR, 2025). Builder/assembly errors and retractable-gear problems dominate; the manufacturer's own view (quoted on Wikipedia) is that early accidents were assembly errors, after which it moved to selling finished/assisted builds. CONFIGURATION: no NTSB finding of deep stall, rain-on-canard or pusher prop strike found. Canard-specific: the canard is a bolt-on surface whose omitted attachment was fatal. Pusher-specific: canopy loss behind which sits the prop (N976DR, no injuries). INFERENCE (mine): the record points to kit complexity (molded carbon, retract system adapted from E-Racer, big engine swap to IO-540 not in the original design) and a very small, high-performance fleet, rather than an aerodynamic flaw. The per-airframe event rate is the worst of the three types here.

why_died_detail: Business failure, not market rejection of the airframe alone: Ronneberg/Murphy partnership (Experimental Aviation, 1989-92) dissolved; lawsuits bankrupted both partners and the corporation; Renaissance Composites (Richard Riley) revived the kit in 1996; Berkut Engineering and Design withdrew it in 2002 and turned to UAVs (Mobius/Geneva Aerospace UAVs on FAA registry); a 2003 sale to Republic Aerospace fell through; owner (named Cruse on Wikipedia) died 22 Aug 2009. Only ~75 kits sold / ~31 built. Also relevant: expensive molded-carbon kit, high-performance 2-seat niche, retractable gear and a poor accident record on a tiny fleet. A revival would have to fix kit build quality/assembly-error exposure and settle unclear IP ownership.

(Ronneberg) -> bankruptcy -> Renaissance Composites (1996) -> Berkut Engineering and Design, Inc. (withdrawn 2002; owner Cruse until death 2009); 2003 Republic Aerospace deal not completed.
